sections.h2: What is the yearly timetable for an Alabama tax sale?
sections.html:
The Alabama Department of Revenue publishes a short property tax timetable: taxes are due October 1 and become delinquent January 1, the file goes to the probate court in February, the probate court meets in March, the property is advertised in April, and the tax sale is held in May. The department's timetable page lists those steps in that order, and its due date page adds that taxes are delinquent after December 31.

MonthStep on the state timetable
October 1Taxes due
January 1Taxes delinquent
FebruaryTurned over to probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilAdvertised for sale
MayTax sale

That calendar is the traditional property sale route. Some counties have moved to a different remedy, covered below, so the month names are a guide and your county's collection office has the real dates for your parcel.

sections.h2: Who can redeem property after an Alabama tax sale, and for how long?
sections.html:
Under Alabama Code section 40-10-120, land bought by the state can be redeemed any time before title passes out of the state. Land bought by anyone else can be redeemed within three years of the sale date.

The list of people who can redeem is wide:

  • The owner, the owner's heirs or personal representatives.
  • Any mortgagee or purchaser of the land or part of it.
  • Anyone with a legal or equitable interest, including a tenant in common.
  • A judgment creditor or other creditor holding a lien.

A minor or a person who is legally incompetent can redeem within one year after the disability is removed, even if the three years have run. A mortgage or lien that was properly recorded at the time of the sale carries an extra right: the holder can redeem within one year from the date written notice of the purchase is served on the holder.

Redemption can also be made of part of the land sold, so long as it covers the whole of the redeeming person's interest. If the same land was sold again for tax in later sales, a person redeeming the first sale has to redeem the later ones at the same time.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to redeem land the state bought?
sections.html:
The redeeming party applies to the county probate judge and deposits what the land sold for, plus interest at eight percent, plus all taxes found due since the sale with eight percent interest, plus officer costs and fees. This is set out in section 40-10-121.

Because the state did not pay later years of tax, the county assessor enters an assessment value for each year after the sale on the application. A person who disagrees can file a written protest with the board of equalization, which sets a hearing after at least 10 days of written notice and certifies the assessed value it fixes to the probate judge.

If any of the land is inside a municipality, the redeeming party also deposits the municipality's unpaid taxes and the amount of municipal tax that went unassessed because the state held the land, with the interest that would have accrued. That is easy to overlook when an owner is trying to estimate a payoff.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to redeem land a private buyer bought?
sections.html:
Section 40-10-122 has the rule for a sale to someone other than the state. The redeeming party deposits with the probate judge the amount the land sold for, plus interest at eight percent per annum from the sale date, and on the part of any excess bid that is 15 percent of assessed market value or less, plus any taxes the purchaser paid with eight percent interest.

If taxes assessed to the purchaser are still unpaid, the redeeming party pays those to the tax collector before redeeming. The party also pays officer costs and fees and a $0.50 fee to the probate judge, and the section allows the application and payment to be made online.

Houses carry extra items. When a residential structure stood on the land at the time of sale, the redeeming party must pay the purchaser the casualty insurance premiums the purchaser paid or owes and the value of preservation improvements, each with eight percent interest. Preservation improvements are those made to keep the property in proper repair.

  • The redeeming party makes a written demand for a statement of improvement value.
  • The purchaser has 10 days to respond with a number.
  • The redeeming party has 10 days to accept it or name a referee.
  • Referees confer, and if they cannot agree they pick an umpire. The majority award is final between the parties.

The redeeming party can take possession before paying those improvement and insurance amounts, but must reimburse them before January 1 of the following tax year or the right in the property is forfeited.

sections.h2: Do all Alabama counties still sell the property itself?
sections.html:
No. An Alabama law passed in 2018, Act 2018-577, gave tax collecting officials the option of selling a tax lien instead of selling the property. The Baldwin County Revenue Commission says it moved to selling liens beginning in 2019 with tax year 2018 delinquent properties, and that all liens for unpaid real property tax are subject to public auction. Its tax lien auction page points bidders to the GovEase platform.

For an owner the practical effect is the same set of questions: how much is owed, who holds the claim, how long is left, and what does it cost to clear it. A lien sale and a property sale call for different paperwork, though, so check with your county revenue office to see which remedy applies to your parcel.

Baldwin County is one example of a county on the lien route. Other counties may still run the traditional sale process, so do not assume the same rules apply across the state.

sections.h2: Which offices handle recording and redemption in a large county like Jefferson?
sections.html:
In Jefferson County the probate court has two divisions that take documents. The Birmingham division is in the Jefferson County Courthouse at 716 North Richard Arrington Jr. Blvd., and the Bessemer division is at 1801 3rd Avenue North in Bessemer. The court's recording FAQ gives hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.

The same page says the recording office cannot run a title search and cannot prepare or revise a deed. It recommends a title company or attorney for lien searches and legal paperwork. Since redemption deposits go to the probate judge, a call to your own county probate office is the right first step for exact amounts.

sections.h2: How does a pending tax sale affect selling the house?
sections.html:
You can generally sell before the sale or during the redemption period if the buyer, or the title company working for the buyer, pays what is owed from the proceeds. The delinquent tax, interest and any redemption deposit become lines on the settlement statement.

Here is what to gather before you talk to a buyer:

  • The parcel number and the tax year or years that are delinquent.
  • Whether the county sold the property or a lien, and on what date.
  • Who bought it: the state or a private purchaser.
  • A payoff figure from the probate judge or tax collector.
  • Any mortgage or lien holders, who may have their own redemption window.

Time is the main enemy. The three year window for a private purchase sounds long, but interest runs the whole time at eight percent, and improvements and insurance the purchaser pays on a house add to the payoff. An as-is cash sale can pay off the redemption amount at closing without waiting on repairs or showings.

faqs.q: When are Alabama property taxes due, and when do they become delinquent?
faqs.a: Taxes are due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31, according to the Alabama Department of Revenue. Its timetable then shows the delinquent file going to probate court in February and a tax sale in May.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem my Alabama property after a tax sale?
faqs.a: Three years from the sale date if a private buyer bought it, and any time before title leaves the state if the state bought it. Section 40-10-120 sets those periods.

faqs.q: What interest rate applies to Alabama tax sale redemption?
faqs.a: Eight percent. Sections 40-10-121 and 40-10-122 both use eight percent interest on the sale price and on the other amounts the redeeming party owes.

faqs.q: Who do I pay to redeem?
faqs.a: You deposit the redemption amount with the judge of probate in the county where the land sits. Section 40-10-122 also allows the application and payment to be made online.

faqs.q: Does the buyer's improvement cost get added when I redeem a house?
faqs.a: For a house, yes in part. The redeeming party reimburses the purchaser's casualty insurance premiums and preservation improvements with eight percent interest. A written demand starts a 10 day exchange, with referees if the two sides disagree on value.

faqs.q: Does every Alabama county run the same kind of tax sale?
faqs.a: No. Since Act 2018-577, collecting officials may sell a tax lien instead of the property. Baldwin County, for example, says it began selling liens in 2019 starting with tax year 2018 delinquents.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house to a cash buyer before the sale or during redemption?
faqs.a: Often yes, if the amount owed can be paid from the sale proceeds and title can be delivered. Get a payoff figure first, and ask an Alabama attorney if a mortgage holder or other lienholder is involved.
